newsitem.title: UK: Oil soars to 5-year high as Iraq tension rises.
newsitem.headline: Oil soars to 5-year high as Iraq tension rises.

text.p: Oil prices soared to their highest level since the Gulf War on Wednesday following an Iraqi missile attack on U.S. fighter planes over northern Iraq and threats of "disproportionate" U.S. retaliation.

World benchmark Brent Blend crude hit $23.82 a barrel -- the highest prompt price on London's International Petroleum Exchange since January 1991's $31.20 posted in the heat of Operation Desert Storm -- before easing back to $23.59 by the close, still 70 cents above Tuesday's close.

Brent left its previous post-Gulf War high of $23.30 in its wake as Middle East tension mounted and the possibility of Iraq returning to the oil market after a six-year absence receded even further, brokers said.

The Pentagon said a surface-to-air missile was fired at two U.S. fighters on Wednesday morning after they were illuminated by Iraqi radar, but did not damage the planes. Washington responded by bolstering its military firepower in the Gulf, calling in B-52 bombers to an Indian Ocean airbase and sending eight F-117A "stealth" fighters to Kuwait.

U.S. defence secretary William Perry warned Iraq that it would soon learn that Washington was "not playing games" and that firing missiles at U.S. planes would draw a response "disproportionate" to the Iraqi attack.
"The oil-for-food deal looks like a receding possibility. Maybe it will have to be 1997 before it's resurrected," said UBS oil analyst Geoff Pyne.

The deal was supposed to allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to raise funds for humanitarian supplies, but it was suspended after Iraqi troops moved into Kurdish areas last week, drawing U.S. retaliatory strikes against targets in the south of the country.

"While there is still a fair chance of further military action, the U.N. cannot deploy its personnel to monitor the limited oil sale. This is the real short-term issue that should concern the markets," said brokers GNI in a daily market report.

While further military action in Iraq poses little significant threat to the region's key oil supplies in Saudi Arabia, Iran and Kuwait, it should continue to deprive a thirsty market of 600-700,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude exports covered by the May 20 U.N. deal.

Italy on Wednesday submitted a draft statement to the Security Council on Wednesday inviting Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to proceed as soon as he can with the oil-for-food deal to relieve the suffering of the Iraqi people.

"Obviously this sort of action takes the wind out of the sails of the Italians and the French... a market which is fairly tight should remain tight," said Charles Gray of oil brokers Prudential Bache Futures.
In anticipation of resumed Iraqi oil sales, some refineries had allowed their stocks to run low and subsequently had to scramble to cover requirements at higher prices.
Industry data released on Tuesday showed U.S. crude stocks fell by more than 6.5 million barrels in the key Gulf coast and east coast refining centres last week.

Heating oil stocks, of increasing importance as the northern hemisphere winter approaches, rose by three million barrels but remain at just 70 percent of levels this time last year in the key northeast U.S. market.
